source: Kannengiesser & Gero (2017) Can Pahl and Beitz' systematic approach be a predictive model of designing? Design Science 3:e24
finding: Protocol analysis (FBS coding) of student design sessions was compared with a simulation of the Pahl and Beitz Systematic Approach. The model predicts some but not all behaviour.
numbers: N=46 sessions: 15 second-year mechanical engineering pairs (45 min each) plus 31 senior-student sessions using brainstorming (10), morphological analysis (11), TRIZ (10). Four measures: first occurrence at start, continuity, linearity (R2>=0.95), slope.
quote: The results indicate that the Systematic Approach can predict some but not all of students' design issue behaviour.
limits: Single university, students only, four assistive-technology tasks, small samples (the 85% threshold was lowered). Tests the process model only, not whether following it gives better designs.
agent_relevance: S1 and S2 as ordered stages describe part of real problem solving. Treat the staged order as a default plan, not a law.

source: Kannengiesser & Gero (2017) Can Pahl and Beitz' systematic approach be a predictive model of designing? Design Science 3:e24 (matches)
finding: Where the staged model fits: requirement, function and expected-behaviour issues appear early in both the model and the students. Structure issues are continuous and linear in both. Structure-issue slopes are very similar for second-year students.
numbers: Evidence from the 15 second-year sessions; R2>=0.95 linearity criterion.
limits: Fit only on some design-issue types.
agent_relevance: Clarify requirements and function before form is a behaviour real solvers show anyway. Cheap to enforce in S1.

source: Kannengiesser & Gero (2017) Can Pahl and Beitz' systematic approach be a predictive model of designing? Design Science 3:e24 (mismatches)
finding: Where the staged model fails: the model says structure and structure-behaviour issues come late, but students raised them early. Requirement and description issues are linear in the model but nonlinear in students.
numbers: Structure-behaviour slopes differ substantially between model and data; for concept-generation groups the model slope is much lower than observed. Early-structure issues appeared in under 85% of sessions for morphological analysis and TRIZ.
limits: Same sample limits as b01.
agent_relevance: Solvers jump to candidate solutions early. A scaffold that forbids early solution talk fights natural behaviour. Better: let S1 and S2 overlap, as the authors suggest, and tag early solutions as hypotheses.

source: Sobek & Ruder (2006) Experimental validation of an improved design method, ASEE 2006-1452
finding: A crossover experiment tested a system-level morphological analysis step added between concept and detail design (the embodiment bridge in Pahl and Beitz). Scores rose after the tool was used.
numbers: 7 teams of 2 in each of groups A and B (one outlier team removed for resisting the tool). Quality score 0-1. Golf-ball problem 0.584 to 0.853 (+46%, p=0.028); mouse problem 0.433 to 0.740 (+71%, p=0.027). Group A +26% (p=0.142, n.s.); group B +97% (p=0.004). Problem difficulty difference n.s. (p=0.331, p=0.366).
limits: Not a true randomised trial: run 2 was always the treatment, so learning, order and experimenter-guidance effects are confounded. Run 2 had more expert interaction. Simple two-hour Lego tasks, tiny N, 5 weeks between runs, one outlier removed. 59% of students rated the tool moderately to very helpful.
agent_relevance: An explicit embodiment-style step (list subfunctions, options, exclusions, interfaces) can help, but was walked through by an experimenter. Supports a coded S2 check on interfaces rather than a prompt line.

source: Sobek & Ruder (2006) Experimental validation of an improved design method, ASEE 2006-1452 (prior finding on telling)
finding: Prior work by the same group found a positive association between system-level design effort and project outcome in senior projects, but simply telling students to consider architecture was not effective.
numbers: Association only (earlier studies cited in the paper); no effect size given in this paper.
limits: Correlation, not causation; cited secondhand here.
agent_relevance: Telling the model to 'consider the architecture' is the weak form. Structured slots filled step by step are the stronger form.

source: Motte, Andersson & Bjarnemo (2005) Teaching a structured design process, ICED05
finding: Students taught a structured engineering design process were compared with an earlier untaught cohort. The structured process helped problem specification, decomposition and criteria specification. Students reached concrete solutions sooner and avoided unproductive feedback loops.
numbers: Report review plus verbal protocol study, before and after the course, plus a third untaught cohort. Sample sizes and statistics not stated on the record page. No correlation was found between process followed and quality of result.
limits: Only the abstract-level record page was read; qualitative; no numbers; no randomisation.
agent_relevance: Staged process saves effort in early stages, but good process did not predict a good result. So a staged scaffold is an efficiency aid, not a correctness guarantee (see G3).

source: Motte, Andersson & Bjarnemo (2005) Teaching a structured design process, ICED05 (heuristic over process)
finding: The heuristic 'think in terms of standard components' seemed to have an important impact on result quality, more than process adherence. Solution searching and solution evaluation needed the most teaching improvement.
numbers: No correlation between observed process and result quality; no numbers reported.
limits: Observation, not a test; abstract-level page only.
agent_relevance: Domain heuristics (reuse standard parts) may carry more value than the stage list. Add such reuse prompts as S2 operators.

source: Daalhuizen, Person & Gattol (2012) The ambiguous role of methods in design education: Delft Method Study, DESIGN 2012
finding: Students told to follow a systematic method (morphological analysis) versus four rules of thumb (primary generator, conjecture-analysis, iteration, satisficing) rated the systematic route more time-pressured, less motivating and less effective. Rated design quality did not differ.
numbers: N=213 (systematic 118, heuristic 95), master's course, two-hour concept task. Time pressure systematic M=4.03 (SD 1.33) vs heuristic 3.23 (SD 1.40), t(211)=4.27, p<.001, d=.59. Effort 4.77 vs 4.49, d=.29, p<.05. Motivation lower under systematic (M=4.43), small effect d about .20. Self-rated effectiveness of approach: heuristic M=5.09 (SD .72) higher, medium-to-large effect. Confidence, conscientiousness, overall design rating: no significant difference.
limits: Self-report outcomes, not blind expert grading of concepts. One brief reported (key manager for elderly). Students, not professionals. Groups did not differ in prior exposure.
agent_relevance: A heavy exhaustive stage procedure cost experience and perceived effectiveness without a measurable quality gain. Prefer a lean scaffold; add exhaustive enumeration only on a failure signal (G1).

source: Daalhuizen, Person & Gattol (2012) The ambiguous role of methods in design education: Delft Method Study, DESIGN 2012 (individual differences)
finding: Cluster analysis of the 213 students gave four process-experience profiles. The method type was not the only driver; past experience, brief perception, motivation and self-confidence mattered.
numbers: Clusters: 31 (14.55%) 'on top of things', 70 (32.86%) 'swamped yet striving', 64 (30.04%) 'indifferent and disconnected', 48 (22.54%) 'lost faith'. Systematic vs heuristic counts: cluster 1 13 vs 18; cluster 2 46 vs 24; cluster 4 28 vs 36 (cluster 3 not read cleanly from the table).
quote: evidence on the role methods play in design is, at best, inconclusive
limits: Exploratory K-means on self-report; one task.
agent_relevance: Moderator: who uses a method matters. For an LLM the analogue is model strength: a stage scaffold may suit weak models and hinder strong ones. Needs measurement per model.

source: Daalhuizen, Person & Gattol (2012) The ambiguous role of methods in design education: Delft Method Study, DESIGN 2012 (earlier German studies, secondhand)
finding: Review of earlier German work: six designers with formal methodological training were compared with two without, and work practices differed markedly. Badke-Schaub and Frankenberger found method use did not guarantee success; factors such as conflict handling were often equally or more important.
numbers: Ehrlenspiel-group comparison: 6 trained vs 2 untrained designers. Cited secondhand; originals not opened.
limits: Tiny N in the original; secondhand description.
agent_relevance: Process quality is only one of several drivers. Do not expect staging alone to carry results; keep checks (G2, G3) as the main lever.

source: Cash, Daalhuizen & Hekkert (2023) Evaluating the efficacy and effectiveness of design methods, Design Studies 88:101204
finding: Systematic review with a 'chain of evidence' from motivation to claims. Across the literature no paper reports every link or consistently follows best practice. The field lacks standards of evidence for claiming a design method works.
numbers: Counts of papers screened not on the page read (abstract page only). 31-page article.
quote: no individual paper either reports all links or consistently achieves best practice
limits: Only the abstract page was read; full text blocked (HTTP 403). No effect sizes available to me.
agent_relevance: The headline claim 'systematic design works' has no solid causal evidence base. In our schema mark S1/S2 staging [S] or [D] and test it on our own tasks.

source: Dillenhofer et al. (2025) Focused competencies in higher education for engineering product development, ICED25
finding: Content analysis of mechanical engineering curricula at three German universities, mapped to the VDI 2221 activity model. Teaching effort concentrates on embodiment ('shaping the modules'); other activities get little.
numbers: Bachelor 210 CP: design-oriented courses 14-26% of workload; master 27-33%. 'Shaping the modules' about 50% of workload tied to product-development activities; other activities average under 10% each. 3 of 19 German universities.
limits: Curriculum study, not an outcome study. Courses identified mostly by title; workload assignment partly subjective.
agent_relevance: VDI 2221 is the working teaching frame in Germany, but its early stages (clarify task, concepts) get least teaching time. Early-stage skill is where scaffolds may add most.

source: Egea et al. (2024) ChatGPT as an inventor: LLMs against humans in engineering design
finding: ChatGPT-4 acted as a design team (instructing two human 'hands') in a 48-hour NERF-launcher hackathon against five human teams. It followed ordinary prototyping practice and ranked second of six.
numbers: Dataset of 116 prototypes. Team 6 (ChatGPT) made 15 physical prototypes, 0.7 h average each. NERF distance: winning human team 37 m, ChatGPT 14.8 m (2nd), then 8.1, 6.6, 5.1, 0.1 m. Chat: 97 prompts, 108 codes.
limits: One hackathon, one task, one run, 30 USD budget, no repeats. Interaction through humans adds noise.
agent_relevance: An unscaffolded LLM already follows explore-then-refine prototyping. Staged structure must beat this baseline, not nothing.

source: Egea et al. (2024) ChatGPT as an inventor: LLMs against humans in engineering design (failure modes)
finding: Weaknesses: the LLM dropped a promising pneumatic concept at minor difficulty, added unnecessary complexity, showed design fixation on details in prompts, and lost continuity. Concept generation was strong.
numbers: Qualitative; the winning team kept pneumatics, the LLM abandoned it after a small hitch (mismatched valves).
limits: Single run; qualitative coding.
agent_relevance: Supports a code-controlled rule: do not abandon a concept on the model's say-so; abandon only on a failed check (G1, G2). Also supports ideation breadth in S2.

source: Egea et al. (2024) ChatGPT as an inventor: LLMs against humans in engineering design (recommendations)
finding: The authors recommend using the LLM for ideation, human oversight for key decisions, iterative feedback loops, prompting for alternatives, and assigning specific subsystem-level tasks.
numbers: Six recommendations; derived from one hackathon.
limits: Not tested as interventions.
agent_relevance: Subsystem-scale tasks match a staged decomposition (S1 then S2). Evidence is weak but consistent with it.

source: Haddad & Seibel (2025) Functional decomposition of technical products based on LLMs and Monte Carlo tree search, ICED25
finding: GPT-4o made functional decompositions (a Pahl and Beitz conceptual-design step) rated about as good as graduate students on completeness and logic, lower on creativity. Adding MCTS raised structural validity but lowered rated completeness and logic.
numbers: Qualitative: 12 usable student decompositions (8 of 20 excluded). Likert means completeness 3.96 GPT-4o, 3.91 students, 3.53 GPT-4o+MCTS-FD; logic 4.00, 3.87, 3.69; creativity 3.12, 3.48 (students best), 3.32. Quantitative: 50 products, 50 FDs per model; error-free 16% GPT-4o vs 42% with MCTS-FD, Llama 405B 10%, Llama 8B 0%; fully connected graphs 44% vs 72%; correct format 100% for GPT-4o.
limits: Students were not scored by the automatic metrics. Metrics are the authors' own graph rules. One product (waffle maker) examined in detail. Input pre-processing needed.
agent_relevance: Code-checked structure (graph rules) lifted error-free output from 16% to 42%: evidence for program-checked S2 steps (G5), with a trade-off in rated quality.

source: Massoudi & Fuge (2025) Agentic LLMs for conceptual systems engineering and design (arXiv 2507.08619)
finding: A nine-role multi-agent system following systems-engineering stages (requirements, function decomposition, embodiment as physics scripts) was compared with a two-agent system on a solar water-filtration design. Output was always well formed but covered few requirements.
numbers: 60 experiments with Llama 3.3 70B and DeepSeek R1 70B, five seeds per configuration. JSON validity 100%; embodiment present 100%; requirement coverage peaked at only 20%. R1 multi-agent about 6 nodes at temperature 1.0, about 650 s per run; best two-agent run 1 node in under 40 s.
limits: One domain; only whether code runs was checked, not physics correctness. First 100k characters of the page read. Spec was given, so requirement elicitation was skipped.
agent_relevance: Format validity is easy; coverage of the real requirements is the hard part. A staged pipeline can look complete and still miss most requirements: needs a requirement-coverage check in code.

source: Qian et al. (2024) ChatDev: communicative agents for software development (ACL 2024)
finding: A waterfall of design, coding and testing phases with role-playing agents beat single-step GPT-Engineer and MetaGPT on a software benchmark. Ablations show each later phase adds quality.
numbers: Completeness / executability / consistency / quality: GPT-Engineer 0.5022/0.3583/0.7887/0.1419; MetaGPT 0.4834/0.4145/0.7601/0.1523; ChatDev 0.5600/0.8800/0.8021/0.3953. Ablation (halting after phase): coding only quality 0.2512; plus code-complete 0.3690; plus review 0.3717; plus testing 0.3953. Removing roles: executability 0.58, quality 0.2212. Removing dehallucination: quality 0.3094.
limits: Quality is a product of three author-defined sub-scores. Own benchmark, GPT-based judging plus human check. Confounds staging with roles and dialogue, so it is not a clean test of staging alone.
agent_relevance: Staged pipeline with verification gives large gains in executability (0.36 to 0.88), mostly via the testing stage (a real check). The check, not the stage list, seems to matter.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why do multi-agent LLM systems fail? (MAST)
finding: Over 1,600 annotated traces from 7 multi-agent frameworks (several are staged-role pipelines such as ChatDev and MetaGPT) show failure rates of 41% to 86.7%. Failures group into system design issues (41.8%), inter-agent misalignment (36.9%) and task verification (21.3%).
numbers: Taxonomy: 14 failure modes in 3 categories, built from 150 traces. LLM annotator agreement with human experts: accuracy 94%. ChatDev on ProgramDev success 33.3% in one setting; MetaGPT has 60-68% fewer FC1 and FC2 failures than ChatDev but 1.56x more FC3 (verification) failures.
limits: Counts depend on annotator model and frameworks; percentages differ between versions of the paper (first version: 11.8% disobey task specification, 12.4% not recognising task completion).
agent_relevance: Rigid role/stage pipelines fail mainly by disobeying their own specification and by weak verification. Supports code-owned transitions and held-out checks (G2, G3).

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why do multi-agent LLM systems fail? (MAST) (interventions)
finding: Fixing role specifications in ChatDev raised success by +9.4%; a cyclic topology with a verification loop (CTO confirms) raised it by +15.6% on ProgramDev. Gains were model-dependent.
numbers: ChatDev + GPT-4o: +9.4% (better role prompts); +15.6% (new topology). AG2 math case: with GPT-4 the improved prompt significantly beat baseline but the new topology did not (Wilcoxon p=0.4); with GPT-4o both were significant (p=0.03). Six repetitions.
limits: Small benchmarks (32 custom tasks, plus HumanEval); gains do not close the gap to strong baselines.
agent_relevance: Adding an iterative verification loop beat polishing the stage prompts. Both effects depend on the base model, so measure on each model we use.

source: Otten et al. (2026) Generative AI in systems engineering: a framework for risk assessment of LLMs (arXiv 2602.04358)
finding: Appeared in search results as a recent systems-engineering risk framework for LLMs. Body text could not be read (PDF unreadable via fetch).
numbers: None read.
limits: Metadata only; not opened.
agent_relevance: Possible source for V-model and VDI 2206 links to LLM risk. Check later.

source: Schiller, Haddad & Seibel (2025) ReqGPT: a fine-tuned LLM for generating requirements documents, ICED25
finding: For the first stage (task clarification, requirements list), a fine-tuned 7B model beat GPT-4 in human ratings against nine ISO 29148 criteria.
numbers: Similarity scores: ReqGPT 77% (IQR 69-86), GPT-4 69% (IQR 62-75), base Mistral 34% (IQR 22-54); p<1%. 107 training lists; 18 graduate students rated outputs in a 60-minute session.
limits: Consumer goods only, small training set generated by GPT-4, student raters, test unnamed. Cites Pahl and Beitz only once; list structure taken from Hubka.
agent_relevance: Requirements clarification can be improved separately from the rest. A requirements check at S1 is feasible. Models still hallucinate requirements.

source: Pahl & Beitz claim as quoted by Daalhuizen et al. (2012)
finding: Founding claim: intuition may rarely give good results, while a systematic method raises the chances of success significantly. Critics (Eder 1998, Frost 1999, Jensen and Andreasen 2010, Dorst 2008) say methods ignore differences in objective, context and actor, and that methods emerge from the design process rather than precede it.
numbers: No numbers in the founding claim. Book not opened; read only as cited by the 2012 paper. Industry use of systematic methods called 'anything but widespread' (Araujo et al. 1996, cited).
limits: Secondhand; book not opened.
agent_relevance: The causal claim behind our S1/S2 rationale rests on authority, not data. Treat as [D] until measured.

source: Daalhuizen, Person & Gattol (2012) The ambiguous role of methods in design education: Delft Method Study, DESIGN 2012 (boundary conditions)
finding: Proposed boundary conditions: a method's effect depends on the type of objective, the context and the actor. Analysis methods are more algorithmic and suit the 'road' view better than synthesis methods.
numbers: Argument based on Dorst (2008) and the study; no numbers.
limits: Argument, not an experiment.
agent_relevance: Staging may fit well-specified analysis-like tasks (code, math) better than open synthesis. Check by task type in our benchmarks.

source: Motte, Andersson & Bjarnemo (2005) Teaching a structured design process, ICED05 (guidance wanted)
finding: Students said they wanted clues and guidance during design; the authors say some steps need deeper, specific experiments.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Abstract-level.
agent_relevance: Guidance at the moment of need, not a fixed schedule, matches G1.

source: Search snippet only: VDI 2221 group-project study of three student brake-system teams (Design Society)
finding: Reported only in a search snippet: three student teams optimised brake systems; one team followed VDI 2221 closely, one only superficially. The authors stress the initial phases and when conceptual decisions are made.
numbers: 3 teams; snippet only.
limits: Not opened; case study.
agent_relevance: Low weight; follow up if full text is wanted.

source: Search snippet only: Diamond of Thought, design-thinking framework for LLMs in wearable design (arXiv 2410.06972)
finding: Staged divergence/convergence framework for LLM design, built from 35 design-thinking models.
numbers: Snippet only.
limits: Not opened; not Pahl and Beitz based.
agent_relevance: Candidate to read next pass for measured LLM results.
